key_insight: A small number of labeled exemplars, retrieved and used alongside textual prompts, can substantially close the gap between zero-shot vision-language segmentation and fully supervised segmentation by providing visual grounding for ambiguous text cues.
problem_solved: Open-vocabulary segmentation suffers from coarse image-level VLM supervision and semantic ambiguity in text prompts; this work tackles whether a few concrete visual examples are enough to bridge that supervision gap for pixel-level predictions.
method: Retrieve a few visually relevant exemplars (images or region crops) for each text query from an external bank using vision-language embeddings.

Augment textual prompts with the retrieved exemplars (or their masks) and use them to guide a segmentation model — via similarity-based pixel classification or lightweight adaptors — so predictions are grounded in concrete visual instances.
Refine or post-process segmentations to reconcile exemplar-specific cues with open-vocabulary categories, improving pixel-level alignment without full dense supervision.
impact: Enables practitioners to achieve near-supervised segmentation performance with only a handful of labeled examples, reducing annotation cost and making open-vocabulary segmentation more practical for real-world, long-tail categories.

paper_title: Retrieve and Segment: Are a Few Examples Enough to Bridge the Supervision Gap in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation?
paper_authors: Tilemachos Aravanis, Vladan Stojnić, Bill Psomas, Nikos Komodakis, Giorgos Tolias
